newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks "honorable compromise" on budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks "honorable compromise" on budget.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Thursday he would seek "an honourable compromise" with congressional Republicans on balancing the federal budget.

"Some of the differences we have are truly principled differences, and we will have to work hard to have an honourable compromise, but i believe that we can do it," Clinton said at a news conference presenting his federal budget for the 1998 fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.

Clinton, a Democrat working with Republican majorities in both houses of Congress, unveiled a $1.69 trillion budget proposal cutting $98.4 billion in taxes over five years yet still reaching balance by 2002. He predicted his plan would keep the U.S. budget in balance for two decades into the future, saying, "We believe we can keep this budget in balance for a good long time."

Despite his conciliatory words a political battle is expected with congressional Republicans over spending priorities, tax cut plans and a Republican-backed proposal to amend the U.S. Constitution to require a balanced budget. Clinton restated his opposition to that on Thursday.
"I do not support a constitutional amendment to balance the budget," he said. "I think it is not necessary or wise and it could have numerous unwanted consequences."

Stalemates over the 1997 budget led to two brief partial shutdowns of federal government operations in late 1995 and early 1996. Many Americans blamed that more on the Republicans than on Clinton, a develpment that has led Republican leaders to sound more conciliatory themselves this time around.
